newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ electricity prices for Oct "reasonable" - EMCO.
newsitem.headline: NZ electricity prices for Oct "reasonable" - EMCO.

text.p: The operator of New Zealand's new wholesale electricity market on Tuesday defended its first month's track record despite persistent price spikes and incomplete data which will force final October prices to be recalculated.
Electricity Market Company (EMCO) said the average North Island price for October was NZ$43.91 per megawatt hour, compared with $32.10 for the South Island.
Prices are subject to revision after national grid operator Transpower failed to supply complete metering data for the month, forcing EMCO to recalculate the prices.
The Market Surveillance Committee earlier described this as an "undesirable situation" and ordered a full report from Transpower.
EMCO Chief Executive Lincoln Gould said: "The final prices are broadly in line with what we expected given demand and hydrological conditions...The averages are quite reasonable, we believe."

Higher North Island prices reflected not just running of more expensive plant than expected, he said, but also higher than usual demand and a fall of some 600 gigawatt hours in available hydro capacity compared with the same time last year.
He told a news conference: "We believe the likely effect of the recalculation will be in general terms a lowering of the final prices that we've announced today."
Transpower omitted to supply data on generation from small suppliers outside the wholesale market which have a combined maximum capacity of 100 megawatts.
But Gould rejected any suggestion that the problem with data from Transpower lent ammunition to critics, such as the Major Electricity Users Group, which questions the market's credibility.
"I think these sort of problems can be well expected, with everyone getting used to the new system. I do not believe it is a huge detriment to the credibility of the market," Gould said.
Of the three types of price spikes seen in October, the market's first month of operation, two had been eliminated from the prices released on Tuesday, Gould said.
The first type were "ramp rate" violations, related mainly to the running of thermal plant and the speed at which its capacity could be adjusted to different output levels.

The second related to anomalies in the pricing model caused by unusual situations, for example when a link between two parts of the transmission system is activated in the midst of one of the half-hour pricing periods.
Gould said, however, there were still cases where prices had spiked up to reflect the fact that more expensive plant than expected was actually run. These prices stood, he said.

The causes were being examined, but related to the inaccuracy of forecast demand as derived from bids and offers in the market. "Certainly there is a considerable urgency in ensuring the regular and continued accuracy of the forecast quantities," Gould said.

He said no fundamental flaws had emerged in the first month of the market's operation but EMCO would like to see the market "settle down" so that price spikes related to the newness of the system disappeared. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473-4746
